url_citation.content:
[# Sid Meier's Memoir!](https://smus.com/books/sid-meiers-memoir) Sid Meier's Memoir! cover

MJ recommended I pick up this book. I regret nothing.

This was a fun look into game development history, narrated by a venerable insider. I remember spending days with AK and MN playing Civ 1 in the mid-90s, and have played every game in the series since.

Billed as a memoir, this book focuses on anecdotes about the games and the game industry, with Sid Meier's personal life taking the backseat. I especially enjoyed the [Nuclear Gandhi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_Gandhi) story. It's such a colorful intersection of a funny premise, computer science, and a hoax.

Sid Meier's taste for non-violent educational simulators is especially compelling, and reading about these games made me really miss them.

...

The intersection of games and education is extremely tricky to pull off, and I would argue that edutainment as a genre has largely failed.

...

One thing the book lacked was specific learnings and insights into game development. The chapter on the failed dinosaur game came closest, but I would have loved a whole book on this. Here are some final notes:

**Follow your interests** : Sid Meier's games have been driven by his personal interests, at least in retrospect.

Sid Meier presents Sid Meier’s Memoir!: A Life in Computer Games

Sid Meier presents Sid Meier’s Memoir!: A Life in Computer Games

In conversation with David Ewalt Presented by Greenlight Books & the NYU Game Center
Legendary game developer Sid Meier brings his signature wit and good humor to the story of his own development in Sid Meier’s Memoir! Over his four-decade career, Meier has produced some of the world’s most popular video games, including Sid Meier’s Civilization , which has sold more than 51 million units worldwide and accumulated more than one billion hours of play. Sid Meier’s Memoir! is the story of an obsessive young computer enthusiast who helped launch a multibillion-dollar industry. Writing with warmth and ironic humor, Meier describes the genesis of his influential studio, MicroProse, founded in 1982 after a trip to a Las Vegas arcade, and recounts the development of landmark games, from vintage classics like Pirates! and Railroad Tycoon , to Civilization and beyond. David Ewalt, award-winning journalist, author, and authority on the intersection of games and technology, joins Meier in conversation at this virtual book talk, co-sponsored by the NYU Game Center.

_Every Friday,_ A.V. Club _staffers kick off our weekly open thread for the discussion of gaming plans and recent gaming glories,

...

The veteran designer talks about _Civilization_ ’s infamous [“Nuclear Gandhi” meme](https://kotaku.com/why-gandhi-is-such-an-asshole-in-civilization-1653818245) . (The story about it being caused by a memory bug is apparently a total fiction, by the way.) He swaps stories about the early days of running his first games company, MicroProse, alongside far more flamboyant former fighter pilot William “Wild Bill” Stealey. He talks about his famous maxim that labels games as “a series of interesting choices.” To some extent, _Memoir!_ —its name itself a reference to the titling tropes of Meier’s games, and the way he eventually became one of the industry’s first (literal) name brands—could just as accurately be titled _Sid Meier Plays The Hits_ .

What it lacks—almost to the point of pathology—is a willingness to indulge in introspection about the actual contents of the games Meier spent his career sticking apostrophe-esses on.

The wide availability of game engines, design tools and art assets (many available for free), has definitely separated the wheat from the chaff when it comes to aspiring game designers. There are many fantastic independent games that have come out over the last fifteen years but also a lot more terrible and/or unrealised ones. As Meier, says, if you’ve got a good concept for a game, then make a simple prototype and demonstrate the potential that way.

Unfortunately, identity politics makes an unwelcome appearance on a few notable occasions within these pages and I think they do need to be addressed. First is his bringing up gender issues:

> Another thing Dan [Bunten] was well ahead of his time on was gender issues. He felt that more designers should be women, and failing that, more designers should be seeking the input of women—and failing _that_ , more designers should at least have a woman’s influence somewhere in their lives.
